circle-parts.why: A circle is every point at a fixed distance from a centre, and its parts have exact names that every circle theorem uses: radius, diameter, chord, tangent, secant, arc, sector. Being precise about the words is what lets you read a theorem.
traps: A diameter is a chord — the longest one — so any fact about chords applies to it too.
A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point. A secant crosses it at two.

circumference-area.why: The circumference is ~2\pi r~ and the area is ~\pi r^{2}~. The number ~\pi~ is just the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter, which is the same for every circle — a fact about circles, not about any particular one.
traps: Only the radius is squared in ~\pi r^{2}~. Squaring ~\pi r~ is a common slip.
When going backwards from an area, divide by ~\pi~ *before* taking the square root.

arcs-sectors.why: An arc and a sector are fractions of the circumference and area. The fraction is the angle over 360. In radians the arc length formula becomes simply ~r\theta~, which is why mathematicians prefer radians.
traps: Arc length uses the circumference and sector area uses the area. The fraction is the same; what it multiplies is not.
Check whether the angle is in degrees or radians before choosing a formula.

circle-angles.why: Angles in circles obey a few precise rules. An inscribed angle is half the central angle on the same arc. All inscribed angles on the same arc are equal. An angle in a semicircle is a right angle. These all follow from isosceles triangles formed by radii.
traps: The inscribed angle is *half* the central angle, never the same size or double.
Spotting a diameter is the trick that unlocks a right angle for free.

chords-tangents.why: A tangent meets the radius at a right angle, so tangent problems become right-triangle problems. Two chords that cross split each other so that the products of their pieces are equal. Each fact gives you one equation to solve.
traps: The distance from an outside point to the centre is the *hypotenuse* of the tangent triangle.
In the crossing-chords rule, multiply the two pieces of the *same* chord together.

circle-equation.why: A circle with centre ~(h, k)~ and radius ~r~ has equation ~(x - h)^{2} + (y - k)^{2} = r^{2}~. It is nothing more than the distance formula saying 'every point is exactly ~r~ from the centre', squared to remove the root.
traps: The signs inside the brackets flip: ~(x + 3)^{2}~ means a centre at ~x = -3~.
The right-hand side is the radius *squared*, so the radius is its square root.
